'''''Hedera colchica''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family ''[[Araliaceae ]]''.<ref name=POWO>{{cite web |url= https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:90679-1 |title= Hedera colchica (K.Koch) K.Koch |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=The Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=April 28, 2025}}</ref><ref name=COL>{{cite web |url= https://www.catalogueoflife.org/data/taxon/3JZ43 |title= Hedera colchica (K.Koch) K.Koch |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Catalogue of Life |publisher=Species 2000 |access-date=April 28, 2025}}</ref> It is native to the Middle East and commonly called '''Persian ivy'''<ref>{{cite web|title=Persian Ivy|publisher=BBC website|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/gardening/plants/plant_finder/plant_pages/370.shtml}}</ref> or '''colchis ivy'''.<ref name=RHS/> It is an [[evergreen]] climbing plant, growing to 30 m high where suitable surfaces (trees, cliffs, walls) are available, and also growing as ground cover where there are no vertical surfaces. It climbs by means of aerial rootlets which cling to the substrate. In warm climates, it grows more rapidly and becomes established faster than other ''Hedera'' species.

==Description==
The leaves are alternate, they are of two types, with palmately five-lobed juvenile leaves on creeping and climbing stems, and unlobed cordate adult leaves, lauroid type, on fertile flowering stems exposed to full sun, usually high in the crowns of trees or the top of rock faces. [[Plant stem|Stem]]s are green.
It has the largest leaves of any ivy to 15 cm wide and 25 cm long.

The flowers are produced from late summer until late autumn, individually small, greenish, produced in large numbers in [[umbel]]s, and very rich in [[nectar]], an important food source for [[bee]]s and other insects. It flowers in September and fruits form during or after winter. The fruits are [[berry (botany)|berries]], globular and black when ripe. They are an important food for many birds. There are one to five seeds in each berry, which are dispersed by the birds swallowing the berries.<ref>{{cite web|title=Plant of the Week on www.davisla.wordpress.com|date=24 January 2012 |url=https://davisla.wordpress.com/2012/01/24/plant-of-the-week-hedera-colchica-dentata-variegata/|accessdate=7 June 2012}}</ref>

The following cultivars have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]:

* ''H. colchica''<ref name=RHS>{{cite web|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=915|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|title=''Hedera colchica'' AGM|accessdate=2013-04-07|archive-date=2019-12-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191210111538/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=915|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 'Dentata', commonly called Bullock's heart ivy, or Elephant's ears.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=3039|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|title=''Hedera colchica'' 'Dentata' AGM|accessdate=2013-04-07}}</ref>
* 'Dentata variegata', synonyms 'Dentata aurea', 'Variegata'<ref>{{cite web|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=916|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|title=''Hedera colchica'' 'Dentata Variegata' (v) AGM|accessdate=2013-04-07}}</ref>
* 'Sulphur heart', synonym 'Paddy's pride'<ref>{{cite web|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=917|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|title=''Hedera colchica'' 'Sulphur Heart' (v) AGM|accessdate=2013-04-07}}</ref>

==Ecology==
It is a woody [[evergreen]] climbing [[shrub]], which can grow in a range of conditions.  It prefers well-drained or [[Alkali soils|alkaline]] soils rich in nutrients and [[humus]] with good water provision, but is extremely tough and adaptable. Like many climbing plants, it prefers its roots in cool shade with its crown in full sun. It can live over 400 years, reaching heights of 30m where suitable surfaces (trees, cliffs, walls) are available. It climbs by means of [[aerial root]]lets with matted pads that cling strongly to the substrate. Its favoured distribution is humid [[microclimate]]s, such as [[cloud forest]], stream valleys, and the mountain ranges on the Turkish coast of the Black Sea, Asia minor, the Persian Gulf, Afghanistan, and some islands of the Red Sea.

==Etymology==
The ancient Latin name for Ivy.<ref name="gledhill">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  pp 114, 193</ref>

Derived from the name ‘Colchis’ or ‘Colchidis’, a Caucasian area once famous for producing poisons.<ref name="gledhill" />
